title: Coordinate Geometry and Straight Lines
objectives: Compute distances and midpoints between points using Pythagoras on coordinate differences
Calculate gradients, build line equations in point-slope and slope-intercept form, and verify them
Determine parallel and perpendicular lines using gradient conditions
Interpret slope and intercept in finance contexts and find break-even intersections of two cost or value lines
motivation: Every chart on a trading terminal is coordinate geometry: price against time, book value against the underlying, cost against volume. A hedge ratio is a slope; two brokers' pricing rules crossing at a volume where their costs agree is an intersection of two lines. This lesson converts pictures into equations, and equations into decisions, with the same tools (Pythagoras, gradients, simultaneous lines) you will reuse throughout the geometry module.

blocks.md: Plot any two quantities against each other and you are working in the coordinate plane: a point is a pair $(x, y)$, a straight line is one linear equation, and questions like 'where do these two pricing rules agree?' become 'where do two lines intersect?'. The payoff of the machinery is translation: a number on a screen (a slope, an intercept, a crossing point) turns into a decision (a hedge size, a fixed cost, a break-even volume).

blocks.text: Distance and midpoint: Pythagoras in the plane

blocks.title: Worked example: from A(1, 2) to B(7, 10)
items: Horizontal change: $\Delta x = 7 - 1 = 6$; vertical change: $\Delta y = 10 - 2 = 8$.
Midpoint: $\left(\frac{1+7}{2}, \frac{2+10}{2}\right) = (4, 6)$ - the average of the coordinates.
Note the 6-8-10 triangle, a scaled 3-4-5. Pythagoras does all the measuring.

blocks.tex: d = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2} \qquad M = \left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2},\ \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)

blocks.text: Gradient: the rate hidden in the line

blocks.md: The gradient $m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ measures how fast $y$ responds to $x$. In finance this slope is rarely mere geometry: a hedge ratio, an option's delta, a beta, each is a gradient of a value line. The line $y = mx + c$ stores the two numbers separately: $m$ is the response rate, and $c$ is the value at $x = 0$, the part that does not respond at all. Reading a chart therefore means asking two questions: how steep, and where does it start?

blocks.title: Worked example: the hedge line
items: A delta-hedged book gains $0.60 for each \$1 rise in the underlying: slope $m = 0.6$. Write $V = c + 0.6S$.
Today the stock is at $S = 100$ and the book is worth \$70: $70 = c + 0.6 \times 100$, so $c = 10$.
Interpretation: $0.6$ is the sensitivity (the delta); $10$ is the stock-independent part of the value.

blocks.caption: The hedge line V = 10 + 0.6S: slope 0.6 is the delta, and the intercept 10 is what the book is worth apart from its stock exposure.

blocks.text: Building the line from two points

blocks.title: Worked example: line through (2, 3) and (6, 11)
items: Verify with the other point: $2(6) - 1 = 11$. Confirmed, a line built from two points must satisfy both.

blocks.md: Parallel lines have equal gradients, same response rate, different starting point. Perpendicular lines satisfy $m_1 m_2 = -1$: each gradient is the negative reciprocal of the other, a fact that falls out of rotating a slope by a right angle. Intersections answer 'where do two rules agree?': set the two expressions equal and solve, exactly the simultaneous-equations skill from the algebra module, now with a picture attached.

blocks.title: Worked example: which broker is cheaper?
items: Broker A charges $300 + 2q$; broker B charges $900 + 0.5q$, costs in dollars for $q$ lots traded.
Decision: below 400 lots A is cheaper, above 400 lots B wins, the intersection is the decision point.

blocks.title: Gradient is a sensitivity
blocks.md: Delta (option value per unit of underlying), beta (stock return per unit of market return), duration (bond price per unit of yield), each is the gradient of a value line. When a risk report says 'the book is short 2,000 deltas', it is quoting the slope of the book's value line, in exactly the $y = mx + c$ language of this lesson.

guidedExercise.prompt: Find the equation of the line through $(-1, 4)$ and $(5, -2)$, verify it against both points, and state where it crosses the x-axis.
hints: Gradient first: both changes are negative here, so watch the signs.
Use point-slope form with either point, then rearrange to $y = mx + c$.
The x-axis crossing means $y = 0$ - solve for $x$.

independentExercise.prompt: Two market-data vendors quote: vendor P charges \$12,000 plus \$15 per connection; vendor Q charges \$30,000 plus \$6 per connection. Write each cost as a line, find the number of connections where costs are equal, compute that common cost, and decide which vendor a 1,000-connection desk should choose.
hints: Set the lines equal and solve for $n$ - a 2x2 system collapsed into one equation.
Evaluate both lines at $n = 1{,}000$ for the decision.

commonMistakes: Dividing the coordinate differences in the wrong order: gradient is $\Delta y / \Delta x$, consistently.
Forgetting that perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$ - 'negative reciprocal', not just 'reciprocal'.
Using the intercept $c$ as a value at some point other than $x = 0$.
Reading an intersection as 'the best choice everywhere', it only marks where two lines switch ranks.
realWorldApplication: Map routing, CAD drafting, sensor triangulation and every line chart in analytics use distance, gradient and intersection of lines as their base operations.
quantFinanceApplication: Hedge ratios, betas and durations are gradients; break-even comparisons between two pricing structures are line intersections, the payoff line of any hedged position is drawn with exactly these tools.
summary: Distance between points is Pythagoras on the coordinate differences; midpoints average the coordinates.
Gradient $m = \Delta y/\Delta x$ is the response rate; $y = mx + c$ separates slope from intercept.
Parallel lines share a gradient; perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$.
Intersections of two lines are decision points, break-evens, cost crossovers, hedge targets, solved by setting the line equations equal.

quiz.prompt: In the hedge line $V = 10 + 0.6S$, what do the slope and the intercept represent?
quiz.modelAnswer: The slope 0.6 is the sensitivity of book value to the stock price (the delta); the intercept 10 is the component of value that does not depend on the stock.
quiz.explanation: Slope is the response per unit of $S$; the intercept is the value when $S = 0$. Together they decompose the book into stock-driven and stock-independent parts.

flashcards.back: $d = \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2}$ - Pythagoras applied to coordinate differences.
$m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$; line $y = mx + c$ with intercept $c$ (value at $x = 0$).
Parallel: equal gradients. Perpendicular: $m_1 m_2 = -1$ (negative reciprocals).
In finance the gradient of a value line is a risk measure: delta, beta and duration are all slopes.
